Barber
BAR-bur
n. (one who shaves the head and beard; in Ezekiel, the razor is a sign of the coming siege)
From Old French barbeor, from Latin barba, a beard. The AV uses the word once, at Ezekiel 5:1, where the prophet is told to take a barber's razor to his own head and beard.

Biblical Definition

Ezekiel's commissions are acted rather than spoken, and this is among the strangest of them: And thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife, take thee a barber's razor, and cause it to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard: then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the hair. The prophet is made into the sign. His own hair is Jerusalem, and the three portions weighed out on the balances are the three ends of the city — a third burned in the midst when the siege is fulfilled, a third smitten with the knife, a third scattered in the wind with a sword drawn out after it.

The horror of the sign depends entirely on what a beard meant in Israel. The priests were forbidden to shave off the corner of the beard or make baldness upon their head; the Nazarite let no razor come upon his head at all for the days of his separation; and when Hanun shaved off half the beards of David's servants it was an act of war. For a priest of the LORD — Ezekiel was one — to take a barber's razor to his own head in public was to enact the stripping of everything that marked Israel as holy and set apart. A barber is an ordinary tradesman. That is the point. The instrument of the judgment was not a sword out of heaven but the commonest blade in the city, applied by a man to himself, in the sight of the people who were about to lose everything the hair stood for.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one whose occupation is to shave men, or to dress and trim their hair.

expand to see more

BARBER, n. One whose occupation is to shave men, or to shave and dress hair.

RAZOR, n. An instrument for shaving off beard or hair.

BEARD, n. The hair that grows on the chin, lips and adjacent parts of the face, chiefly of male adults.

BALDNESS, n. The want of hair on the top of the head; loss of hair.

BALANCE, n. A pair of scales, for ascertaining the weight of bodies.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 5:1 — "And thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife, take thee a barber's razor, and cause it to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard: then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the hair."

Ezekiel 5:2 — "Thou shalt burn with fire a third part in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are fulfilled: and thou shalt take a third part, and smite about it with a knife: and a third part thou shalt scatter in the wind; and I will draw out a sword after them."

Leviticus 21:5 — "They shall not make baldness upon their head, neither shall they shave off the corner of their beard, nor make any cuttings in their flesh."

Numbers 6:5 — "All the days of the vow of his separation there shall no razor come upon his head: until the days be fulfilled, in the which he separateth himself unto the LORD, he shall be holy, and shall let the locks of the hair of his head grow."

Modern Corruption

The prophetic sign-acts are read as theatre or as symptoms rather than as commanded obedience, and the cost to the man who performed them disappears.

expand to see more

A reading now common treats Ezekiel's sign-acts — the shaved head, the tile, the four hundred and thirty days on his side, the untouched tears at his wife's death — as evidence of the prophet's psychological state rather than as obedience to explicit commands. The text will not support it. Every one of them is introduced by a direct word from the LORD and interpreted immediately afterward by the LORD, and the prophet's own reaction is recorded when he has one. To file the barber's razor under pathology is to lose the whole point of the office: God made the messenger into the message, and the messenger bore it.

The second loss is the weight of the sign for a priest. Ezekiel was of the priestly line and knew Leviticus 21 by heart. To put a razor to his head was to do in public the thing his order was forbidden to do, and to do it as a picture of what was about to happen to the holy city. The principle to recover is that God's servants have been asked for costly obedience in the currency they value most — Abraham the son, Hosea the marriage, Ezekiel the beard — and none of them was told to do it for effect. They were told to do it because the word was true and the people would not hear it spoken.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gallab (H1532), a barber; taar (H8593), a razor; zaqan (H2206), the beard.

expand to see more

Hebrew gallab (H1532) — a barber; used once in the Old Testament, in Ezekiel's sign-act.

Hebrew taar (H8593) — a razor, from a root meaning to lay bare; the same word forbidden to the Nazarite.

Hebrew zaqan (H2206) — the beard; the mark of a man's dignity, and in Israel of his consecration.

Hebrew mozen (H3976) — a balance, scales; on which the hair of the city was weighed into thirds.

Hebrew qorchah (H7144) — baldness; forbidden to the priests in Leviticus 21:5 as a heathen mourning rite.

Usage

"“take thee a barber's razor” — the commonest blade in the city made a prophecy."

"“then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the hair” — Jerusalem weighed into three ends."

"“there shall no razor come upon his head” — what the sign-act deliberately violated."
